meaning.text: Afanasyev glosses Usud with the Russian Sudba ('Fate') when retelling the Serbian tale.

Afanasyev says the word sudba (Serbian usud, sudjenje, as in 'tako ti je usud usudio!') shares a root with the verb 'to judge', and so means what is adjudged or predestined to a person by a higher divine judgment.

scene.text: In the Serbian tale of Fate and the two Dolyas, the wanderer finds Usud living richly and merrily in a large palace.
In the tale, Usud afterwards grows poorer with each day, and its house smaller and sadder.
In another Serbian tale the hero, going to Fate to have hard questions answered, comes to a water and must call on it to carry him across.

behavior_habitat.text: Every night Usud assigns to the infants born during the past day exactly the same lot that it itself enjoyed in the day just gone.
In the tale, a man's Dolya, asked who gave her to him, answers that Fate (Usud) did.
People the wanderer meets on the road beg him to find out from Usud about their own lot.
Usud tells the poor brother that he was born on an 'orphan's night' and that such is his lot.
In another Serbian tale Usud answers the hero's question why a water has no yield: because it has never drowned a person.
Usud warns the hero not to tell the water the answer until it has carried him across, or it will drown him at once.
Usud and Sreća appear in a further tale, printed in the Matica edition, as living beings who stand under God's commands.

dealing_with_it.text: Usud advises the unlucky brother to take in his brother's daughter Militsa, born in a happy hour, and to call everything he gains hers rather than his own; following this counsel, he lives in plenty.
When he forgets and calls his grain 'mine', his field bursts into flame, and the fire dies as soon as he says the grain belongs to his niece Militsa.

rationale.text: Every surviving clause rests on Afanasyev's Poetic Views of the Slavs (volumes 2 and 3, counted as one source), retelling Serbian tales.

Afanasyev says the tale of Fate and the two Dolyas is printed in Karadžić's Serbian tales, and points to a further tale in the Matica edition; neither is a source in this entry, so no second independent author supports a clause.
The verified entry names one people, the Serbs.
One 19th-century compiler and one people give the grade literary: a lone compiler printing collected tales still counts as one source, so the entry cannot reach regional on this corpus.

notes.text: appearance: no source describes Usud's body; Afanasyev 1869 p.410 describes the Dolyas (a fair maiden spinning gold thread, a grey old woman asleep) but not Usud itself. Searched usud, усуд, усуди, усудио, усуда, destiny, fate across all sources; Machal pp.250-252 discuss fate spirits but do not name Usud.
origin: no opened page says where Usud comes from or who becomes one. Searched usud, усуд, усуда, усуди in all sources.

names.variants: no opened page gives another name for the being; Karadzic 1852 (leaf 739) lists судбина and судиште as words for fate cf. усуд, but as abstract nouns, not names of the being, so they are not recorded.
variants: the only sources are two Serbian tales retold by Afanasyev; no regional or people-specific variants are described.

Karadzic 1852 prints a headword 'Усуд, m. тако ти је усуд усудио (у приповијеци)' on leaf 807 (page 792), but the tag karadzic1852:s.v.Усуд resolves to leaf 739, where 'усуд' first opens a line as a cross-reference under судиште. The entry is therefore not cited; the same phrase is cited through Afanasyev 1869 p.370. A headwords override (Усуд -> leaf 807) would fix the resolution.
Afanasyev refers to the being as Судьба (Fate) with Усуд in parentheses; the clauses read his Судьба in these Serbian tales as Usud. In the 1868 p.234 tale the Serbian text names Усуд directly.

Verify: graded literary because the only source in the corpus is Afanasyev, who retells Serbian tales from Karadžić's collection and a Matica edition (afanasyev1869:pp.409-410); opening those collections directly would add an independent source and could raise the grade to regional.
